title: Knowledge check: Selecting and Filtering Data

questions.prompt: For “Selecting and Filtering Data”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: Data transformations should be explicit and auditable: define the rule, check row counts and keys, and preserve the reason for each cleaning choice. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Selecting and Filtering Data” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Selecting Columns” as part of lesson 106. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Selecting and Filtering Data” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Compare before/after row counts, check a key or range invariant, and record how missing or duplicate records were handled. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
